A short course in one lesson · Companion to The House of Timur

Timur in the European Imagination

From the embassy to Samarkand to Marlowe, the opera house, and the national hero of Uzbekistan, 1402 to today

Prepared for Tom Goldberger · September 2026

Timur (1336–1405) never set foot in Christian Europe. His furthest campaigns in the west took him to Smyrna on the Aegean coast in December 1402. Yet for six centuries Europeans wrote about him, painted him, set him to music and argued over him. The "Tamerlane" of European books and stages is only loosely tied to the Central Asian conqueror you met in The House of Timur. He is a series of reinventions, and each one tells you more about the Europeans who made it than about Timur himself.

This lesson follows five of those reinventions in order: the useful ally of the first diplomatic reports; the humanists' lesson in Fortune and the caged sultan; Marlowe's aspiring "Scythian shepherd"; the political symbol of the Baroque stage and the Enlightenment historians; and the orientalist, Soviet and post-Soviet Timurs of the last two centuries. It should take about 45–60 minutes to read.

How to read the claims. Dates are CE and have been checked against published sources, which are listed at the end. Where a traveller or chronicler reports something that cannot be verified, the claim is credited to that writer. Two famous stories, Bayezid's iron cage and the "curse" of Timur's tomb, are marked as legends, with what is known about where they came from. The spelling varies with the source: Timur, Temür, Tamerlane, Tamburlaine, Tamerlano, Tamorlán. They all mean the same man.

1The lesson

Timur in the European imagination, 1402 to today

Five sections · about 45–60 minutes · 2 maps, 1 chart, 10 images

Why it matters

Europe's Tamerlane is one of the best case studies of how a real person becomes a portable myth. He was a rescuer of Christendom, then a moral warning, then an emblem of ambition, then a stand-in for William III, and finally a warning against conquest itself. Following the changes teaches you to ask of any historical image: who made this, when, and what did they need it for?

1. News from Ankara: allies, envoys and a captive, 1402–1427

By 1402 the Ottoman sultan Bayezid I, called Yıldırım ("the Thunderbolt"), was the most feared ruler in the eastern Mediterranean. In September 1396 he had destroyed a crusading army under Sigismund of Hungary at Nicopolis on the Danube, and since 1394 he had been blockading Constantinople. Then, on 28 July 1402, Timur crushed Bayezid's army near Ankara and took the sultan prisoner. Bayezid died in captivity in March 1403, and his sons fought one another for a decade (the "Ottoman Interregnum"). The pressure on Constantinople lifted. The city would hold out for another half-century, until 1453.

So Europe's first Tamerlane was not a monster but a deliverer. He was a distant enemy of Europe's enemy who might be drawn into an alliance. Two Christian courts had already sent envoys to him, and he answered both.

Castile: two embassies and a book

King Henry III of Castile had sent two envoys east before the battle. According to Clavijo's later narrative, Payo Gómez de Sotomayor and Hernán Sánchez de Palazuelos were with Timur at Ankara and saw the victory. Timur sent them home with his own ambassador, called Muhammad al-Qazi in the Castilian sources, with letters and gifts. Among the gifts, it is reported, were two women from Bayezid's household.

Henry replied with a second, larger embassy led by his chamberlain Ruy González de Clavijo, a Madrid nobleman, with the Dominican friar Alonso Páez de Santa María and the royal guard Gómez de Salazar. They sailed from Cádiz in late May 1403 (the published dates are 21 or 22 May), by way of the Balearics, Gaeta and Rhodes to Constantinople, where they spent the winter. On 20 March 1404 they set out across the Black Sea and landed at Trebizond on 11 April. Timur had already left the Caucasus for home, so the Castilians chased him across Anatolia, Iran and Khorasan, stopping only a night or two in most towns. They reached the outskirts of Samarkand on 4 September 1404.

Clavijo's account is the fullest description of Timur's court by any European. He describes audiences in garden palaces, silk pavilions hung with jewels, and elephants. He watched Samarkand being built and rebuilt. In the translation by Guy Le Strange (1928), Timur finds fault with the gateway of the great mosque built in memory of "the mother of his wife." Clavijo writes that "no sooner had it been completed than he began to find fault with its entrance gateway, which he now said was much too low and must be pulled down." He also reports that the envoys of the Ming emperor were seated below the Castilians, and that Timur called the Chinese ruler a thief and a bad man to Clavijo's face.

By Clavijo's account, the old conqueror was ill, and the embassy was told to leave on 18 November without a farewell audience. (Persian sources say Timur did receive and dismiss them.) They left on 21 November 1404. Timur died at Otrar in February 1405, on the march to China, while the Castilians were still on their way home. In the turmoil that followed, they were held at Tabriz until mid-August 1405. They reached Trebizond on 17 September and Constantinople on 22 October, sailed on to Genoa, and reported to the king on 24 March 1406.

The point to notice is the delay. Clavijo's careful, concrete observations were not printed until 1582, in Seville, and did not appear in English until 1859. The Europeans who shaped the popular image of Tamerlane in the sixteenth century mostly did not use the one detailed eyewitness report their own culture had produced.

France: a letter, an archbishop and a question of authenticity

Timur's other European correspondent was Charles VI of France. The messenger was a Dominican, John (Jean), archbishop of Sultaniyya in north-western Iran, who reached Paris on 15 June 1403. He brought a letter in Persian dated 1 Muharram 805 (1 August 1402), a few days after Ankara, together with Latin and French versions. The letter offered friendship and asked that merchants be protected in both directions. Charles VI's Latin reply, also from June 1403, survives in the French archives. John also wrote a short account of Timur and his court (1403), which a French royal chronicle partly absorbed, and a longer description of the East, the Libellus de notitia orbis (1404).

Recent scholarship has made this story more complicated. Abolala Soudavar (2013) argued that the Persian letter kept in the Archives nationales is a forgery. In his view it was made by John or someone in his circle, whose Persian was poor, to give weight to a mission from which John gained gifts and prestige at every court he visited. The argument is recent, but it is a useful warning. Even Europe's "direct" contact with Timur passed through intermediaries who had their own interests.

Bavaria: Johann Schiltberger, a captive in two armies

The third early witness was not a diplomat but a prisoner. Johann (Hans) Schiltberger, born in 1380 near Freising in Bavaria, was wounded and captured at Nicopolis in 1396, aged about sixteen. He served Bayezid for six years as a runner. After Ankara he passed into Timur's hands and then, after 1405, to Timur's sons and grandsons. He later went with a Tatar prince into the steppe and to the Volga. He escaped around the Black Sea and reached home in 1427.

His Reisebuch was printed at Augsburg in the later fifteenth century, and several editions followed in the fifteenth and sixteenth centuries. It gave German readers a view of Ankara and its aftermath from inside both armies. It is also a warning about memory. Schiltberger wrote more than twenty years after the events, and his chapters on Timur are brief, muddled in chronology and sometimes fabulous. His editors have long noted this. It was an English translation for the Hakluyt Society in 1879 that brought him to a wider modern readership.

Why it matters

Europe's first Tamerlane was a strategic figure. He was valued because he broke the Ottomans. The earliest reports are also the most down-to-earth, full of roads, gifts, audiences and dates. Everything later adds colour, moral lessons and legend. When a later text says something that none of these witnesses mentions, that is a reason to be suspicious.

2. The humanists' Tamerlane: Fortune's wheel and the caged sultan, c. 1440–1600

Italian humanists turned Timur into an exemplum, a story from history that teaches a moral. In his dialogue De varietate fortunae ("On the Vicissitudes of Fortune," completed around 1447–48), the Florentine scholar Poggio Bracciolini used Timur's career to show how Fortune raises and throws down the great. Gibbon, reading Poggio three centuries later, noted that he ranked Timur with "the illustrious Barbarians of antiquity" and said he had his information from people who had been in the East.

The figure who fixed the shape of the story for Europe, however, was the defeated sultan. For humanist writers the most important thing about Tamerlane was what he did to Bayezid.

Legend: Bayezid in the iron cage

What the story says. After Ankara, Timur kept Bayezid in an iron cage and carried him about on campaign. He used the sultan as a footstool or a mounting block, fed him scraps under the table, and made his wife serve at the victory feast unveiled. Bayezid, in despair, killed himself by dashing his head against the bars.

What can be established. Bayezid was captured at Ankara and died in captivity in March 1403. That much is not in doubt. Timur's own court historians describe him receiving the sultan courteously. Beyond that, the story grew in the telling:

  • Marcus Milwright and Evanthia Baboula (2011) found no firm contemporary confirmation of a literal cage. Early accounts often leave it out or describe a different kind of confinement.
  • Some Ottoman chroniclers of the later fifteenth and early sixteenth centuries do mention a kafes ("cage"). Mehmed Neşri (d. c. 1520) has Timur ask Bayezid what he would have done with a captive Timur. "Put him in an iron cage," Bayezid answers, and so the cage is made. Some historians have suggested that a barred litter used to move a prisoner lies behind the word.
  • In Latin Europe, Aeneas Silvius Piccolomini, later Pope Pius II (r. 1458–64), gathered most of the humiliation motifs in his Asia (1450s–60s): the cage, the scraps under the table, the sultan as mounting block. The Greek-Italian writer Theodore Spandounes shows the story still growing. His Italian text of 1509 has only golden chains and the footstool, and the cage appears in later versions.

Verdict. Treat the cage as a legend whose details were elaborated in Europe. Its appeal was political as much as moral: it showed the Turkish sultan humbled. Section 4 shows the Enlightenment arguing over whether it was true, and Milwright and Baboula follow that debate into the twentieth century.

From miscellany to biography

Two sixteenth-century books did most to spread Tamerlane through Europe.

The first was the Silva de varia lección ("A Miscellany of Various Readings") by Pedro Mexía of Seville, first published there in 1540. It was a bestseller: it was reprinted seventeen times in the sixteenth century and translated into Italian (1542), French (1552) and English (1571). Its chapter on Tamerlane gave readers across Europe a compact story. In it, a man of humble birth rises to empire by courage and a severe kind of justice. Marlowe would make him a shepherd. Mexía's Tamerlane also sets out tents before a besieged city: white for mercy on the first day, red for death to the men of fighting age on the second, black for death to all on the third. Marlowe put these tents on stage too.

The second was a full Latin biography, Magni Tamerlanis Scythiarum imperatoris vita ("The Life of the Great Tamerlane, Emperor of the Scythians"), by the Italian Pietro Perondino (Petrus Perondinus), printed in Florence in 1553. "Scythian" was the classical name for the nomads of the northern steppe. Calling Timur a Scythian placed him in a literary line that reached back to Herodotus, and it hid the actual Turko-Mongol and Islamic world of Transoxiana. The same years produced the image of him that still hangs in the Uffizi.

At the end of the century the French writer Jean du Bec published an Histoire du grand empereur Tamerlanes (Rouen, 1595). An English version followed in 1597. Du Bec claimed to be following an Arabic life by a companion of Timur called "Alhacen," but modern scholars read the book as closer to heroic fiction than to biography. By 1600, then, a European reader could find Tamerlane as a moral lesson, as a romance hero, and as a scourge of the Turks, but hardly anywhere as the Timur of Samarkand.

Why it matters

The humanists gave Tamerlane the two features that later writers kept: the low-born man raised by Fortune, and the proud sultan humbled. Neither depended on new information from Asia. They came from the classical habit of reading history as moral example, and from a Europe that wanted to see the Ottomans brought low.

3. Marlowe's "Scythian shepherd," 1587–88

The most famous European Tamerlane was written by a Cambridge graduate in his early twenties. Christopher Marlowe's Tamburlaine the Great was written and staged in London in 1587 or 1588 by the Lord Admiral's Men. The prologue to Part 2 presents it as a sequel prompted by the success of Part 1. Both parts were entered in the Stationers' Register on 14 August 1590 and printed together that year, anonymously. Modern scholars attribute them to Marlowe with near-unanimity.

What Marlowe took and what he changed. Scholars since Ethel Seaton in the 1920s have traced his sources. He used Mexía's chapter, in the English of Thomas Fortescue's The Foreste (1571) and George Whetstone's The English Myrror (1586). He used Perondinus's Latin Vita (1553), especially for Bajazeth. For his geography he used Abraham Ortelius's atlas Theatrum orbis terrarum (1570). From these he took the shepherd origin, the coloured tents before Damascus, and the caged Bajazeth. Marlowe did not invent the legend, but his staging made it unforgettable. Bajazeth is kept in a cage, fed scraps from Tamburlaine's table and used as a footstool. At last he beats out his brains against the bars, and his wife Zabina does the same.

Other changes are Marlowe's own. The historical Timur was a Muslim Turkic nobleman of the Barlas tribe. Marlowe's hero is a pagan herdsman who conquers by force of will and rhetoric. His men are named Techelles, Usumcasane and Theridamas. The Persian kings Mycetes and Cosroe are loosely based, it has been suggested, on the warring Muzaffarid brothers of Shiraz. Marlowe is also harsher to Bajazeth and warmer to Tamburlaine than his sources are.

I that am term'd the scourge and wrath of God,
The only fear and terror of the world,
Will first subdue the Turk, and then enlarge
Those Christian captives which you keep as slaves…Tamburlaine to Bajazeth, Tamburlaine Part 1, Act 3

"Scourge of God" was an old label, already attached to Attila. It carries a double meaning. A scourge is sent by God to punish the wicked, here the Turks, but it is still only an instrument, and instruments are thrown away. Part 2 pushes this to the limit. Tamburlaine has his chariot drawn by captive kings ("Holla, ye pampered jades of Asia!"), orders the drowning of Babylon's people, burns the Qur'an, and defies God. Then he falls sick and dies, sending his sons to finish conquering the world. Critics still argue whether the play celebrates the "aspiring mind" or punishes it.

Reception. The play was a hit and set a fashion for thundering Eastern conquerors and blank verse that carried a full line of sense. Ben Jonson later praised "Marlowe's mighty line." Not everyone approved. In 1588 Robert Greene sneered at "that atheist Tamburlan." Shakespeare parodied the "pampered jades" in the ranting of Pistol in 2 Henry IV. For the history of Timur's image, the key fact is that Marlowe's version reached far more people than any history book. For English speakers, "Tamburlaine" came to mean the insatiable conqueror.

Why it matters

Marlowe made Tamerlane a vehicle for questions that had nothing to do with Central Asia: can a man make himself by will alone, what are the limits of power, and is conquest divinely sanctioned? The "Scythian shepherd" who beats kings was a provocation in a society of fixed ranks. That is why the play still gets revived, and why its Timur is almost wholly European.

4. Baroque and Enlightenment: Whig hero, operatic lover, a fable on trial, 1636–1788

In the seventeenth and eighteenth centuries Europeans gained access, for the first time, to the Timurid-era Islamic histories. In 1636 the Leiden orientalist Jacobus Golius printed the Arabic text of Ibn Arabshah's life of Timur. Ibn Arabshah (1389–1450) was a native of Damascus who had been carried off to Samarkand as a boy after Timur took the city, and he finished his hostile, florid book in 1435. In 1722 a French translation by François Pétis de la Croix of Sharaf al-Din Ali Yazdi's Zafarnama, the admiring Persian court history written for Timur's descendants, was published in Paris. Europe now had the two opposite Islamic portraits side by side: a monster in Ibn Arabshah and a hero in Yazdi.

The stage: Tamerlane the good king

The stage preferred the hero. In France, Nicolas Pradon's tragedy Tamerlan, ou la Mort de Bajazet (1675–76) turned Timur into a gallant gentleman. In England, Nicholas Rowe's Tamerlane opened at the Lincoln's Inn Fields theatre in December 1701, with Thomas Betterton in the title role. Rowe was a committed Whig, and his play was an allegory of the politics of the day:

  • Tamerlane is a moderate, tolerant, lawful prince who stands for King William III.
  • Bajazet is the arrogant tyrant who stands for Louis XIV of France.
  • The play came as war with France approached, just after Louis recognised the son of the exiled James II as king of England.

It became a political ritual. The play was performed each year on or around 4 November (William's birthday) or 5 November (the anniversary of his landing in 1688, and also Guy Fawkes night). It was not staged in London under the Tory ministry of 1710–14. In Dublin in November 1712 a performance with a provocative prologue caused a riot. After Addison's Cato, it was reckoned the most performed tragedy of the eighteenth-century stage apart from Shakespeare. Marlowe's shepherd who defied heaven had become a constitutional monarch.

The opera house: Bajazet steals the show

Italian opera took the same plot of conqueror, captive sultan, and daughter in between, and moved the sympathy towards Bajazet:

  • Francesco Gasparini, Tamerlano, Teatro San Cassiano, Venice, 24 January 1711. The libretto was by Agostino Piovene, after Pradon. Unusually, Bajazet was sung by a tenor, not a castrato. Gasparini reworked the opera as Il Bajazet for Reggio Emilia in 1719, with the tenor Francesco Borosini, and added an on-stage suicide.
  • George Frideric Handel, Tamerlano, King's Theatre, Haymarket, London, 31 October 1724. The libretto was by Nicola Haym, after Piovene. Borosini brought Gasparini's 1719 score to London and sang Bajazet. The premiere fell just before the annual Rowe performances in early November. Bajazet has been called the first great tenor role in opera.
  • Antonio Vivaldi, Bajazet (also called Il Tamerlano), Verona, Carnival season 1735, again to Piovene's libretto.

The historians: is the cage a fable?

The Enlightenment put the cage legend on trial. In his Essai sur les mœurs (1756), chapter 88, Voltaire pointed out that none of the Persian or Arab lives of Timur says he shut Bayezid in an iron cage, while the Turkish annals do. He asked whether they meant to make Tamerlane odious or had copied Greek historians. He dismissed as a "fable" the related story that later sultans stopped marrying because of the insult to Bayezid's wife, noting the marriages of Murad II and Mehmed II.

Edward Gibbon answered in chapter 65 of the Decline and Fall (vol. 6, 1788). He admitted that "modern writers" rejected the iron cage "as a fable." Against them he set a "chain of witnesses": the biographer of Marshal Boucicault, Poggio, Ibn Arabshah, the Byzantine historian Phrantzes, and the Turkish annals. He treated the cage as credible. The disagreement shows two methods at work. Voltaire weighed which kind of source was likely to lie. Gibbon counted independent witnesses. Modern historians side more with Voltaire's caution, although, as Section 2 showed, the question is about how and when the story formed rather than a simple yes or no.

Why it matters

In a century, Tamerlane went from Marlowe's blasphemer to a model of lawful kingship in London and a lovesick tyrant in Venice. Meanwhile the new Arabic and Persian sources allowed the first critical debates about what really happened. The theatre used Timur as a mirror for European politics, and the historians began, slowly, to use him as a subject of history.

5. Poets, painters, scientists and a nation, 1827 to today

The romantic Tamerlane

In 1827 an anonymous forty-page pamphlet, Tamerlane and Other Poems "by a Bostonian," appeared in Boston. It was the first book of the eighteen-year-old Edgar Allan Poe. Poe is American, but his Tamerlane belongs to the same European literary tradition. In the title poem (406 lines in 1827, cut to 234 by 1845), the dying conqueror confesses to a friar that he gave up love for ambition. Poe admitted in his notes that he knew little about the historical Tamerlane "and with that little, I have taken the full liberty of a poet." By now the name worked as a symbol that needed no history.

The pyramid of skulls

In the 1860s the Russian empire conquered much of Central Asia; its forces took Samarkand, Timur's capital, in 1868. The painter Vasily Vereshchagin travelled with the army. In Munich in 1871 he painted The Apotheosis of War: a pyramid of skulls under a hot sky, with crows, in front of a ruined city. The painting is in the Tretyakov Gallery in Moscow. According to the Russian Wikipedia account, it was originally called The Triumph of Tamerlane, and Timur's armies are known in the chronicles for building towers of heads. On the frame Vereshchagin had it inscribed that the painting was dedicated "to all great conquerors, past, present and to come." At this point Tamerlane stood for conquest in general, including the conquest Russia had just made of his homeland.

Opening the tomb, 1941

In June 1941 a Soviet team including the anthropologist Mikhail Gerasimov opened Timur's grave in the Gur-e Amir mausoleum at Samarkand. Published accounts give 19 or 20 June for the opening. The skeleton bore out the old nickname "Timur the Lame": the right leg and right arm showed old injuries, and the knee had fused so that the leg stayed bent. Gerasimov's reconstruction of the skull gave the world its first scientifically grounded face of Timur. He was about 172–173 cm tall, above average for his time. On 22 June 1941, within days of the opening, Germany invaded the Soviet Union.

Legend: the curse of Timur

A well-known story says the tomb carried the warning "When I rise from the dead, the world shall tremble." A second inscription found inside supposedly threatened that whoever opened it would unleash an invader more terrible than Timur. Local elders are said to have warned the scientists, and the German invasion is said to have followed as punishment. Stalin, the story goes, had the body reburied with Islamic rites, and the tide turned at Stalingrad. The reburial did take place, in late 1942 (sources give November or 20 December). But people close to Gerasimov have called the inscription story a fabrication, and there is no evidence of a causal connection. Treat it as a legend: a modern myth that turned a scientific exhumation into a tale of omen and punishment.

From scourge to founding father

After Uzbekistan became independent in 1991, its government made Amir Temur, as he is called there, the country's national hero. On 31 August 1993, the eve of the second anniversary of independence, a bronze equestrian statue of Timur by the sculptors Ilkhom and Kamol Jabbarov was unveiled in central Tashkent. It stands on the site where a monument to Karl Marx had stood since 1968. President Islam Karimov declared 1996 the "Year of Amir Temur" for the 660th anniversary of his birth, and the State Museum of Timurid History opened in Tashkent on 18 October 1996. Statues in Samarkand and Shahrisabz followed the same year. The pedestal of the Tashkent statue carries the motto "strength is in justice."

This Timur is almost the opposite of Europe's. He is not a scourge or an over-reacher, but a state-builder, lawgiver and patron of Samarkand's architecture and learning, and a symbol of statehood older than Russian or Soviet rule. Commentators have pointed out that Timur has, in the words of one survey of Tashkent's monuments, only "tenuous historical links to modern conceptions of Uzbek identity." The Uzbeks, after all, were the people who drove his descendants out of Transoxiana in the early sixteenth century (see The House of Timur, Lesson 6). But this image too is a reinvention made for the needs of its makers, just as Rowe's William III and Vereshchagin's warning were.

Why it matters

By the twentieth century the question "who was Timur?" had split in two. For Europeans he had become a metaphor for ambition, romance, and war. In Central Asia he became a national ancestor. Science, in the form of Gerasimov's skeleton, confirmed a few plain facts, and a legend grew up around the dig anyway. Comparing the two traditions shows that every culture remembers conquerors in the way that serves its own story.

Conclusion: six Tamerlanes

Put the images side by side. In 1402–06 he was the useful ally who broke the Ottomans and received embassies. From the 1440s to the 1590s he was the moral example, the low-born favourite of Fortune who caged a proud sultan. In 1587–88 he was Marlowe's aspiring mind, the scourge of God who defied God. In the eighteenth century he was the good king of the Whigs, the rival in love on the opera stage, and a problem of evidence for Voltaire and Gibbon. In the nineteenth century he was a symbol of romantic ambition and of war itself. Since 1991 he has been the founding hero of Uzbekistan. The historical Timur of Manz's and Marozzi's biographies, the Barlas amir who ruled from Samarkand, sits underneath all of them and rarely shows through.

Review questions

Try each one first, then open it to check the answer.

1Why did news of the battle of Ankara (1402) make Timur look like a friend to Europeans, and what practical steps did Castile and France take?
Answer. Timur had defeated and captured Bayezid I, whose armies had crushed the crusade at Nicopolis (1396) and who had been blockading Constantinople since 1394. The Ottoman collapse relieved Constantinople and raised hopes of an alliance. Henry III of Castile had envoys at Ankara and then sent Clavijo's embassy (1403–06). Charles VI of France received Timur's envoy, the Dominican John of Sultaniyya, in June 1403 and sent a reply.
2What makes Clavijo's narrative so valuable, and why did it have so little effect on the sixteenth-century image of Tamerlane?
Answer. It is the most detailed first-hand European description of Timur's court and of Samarkand in 1404, full of concrete observations (audiences, gardens, building works, the seating of the Ming envoys). But it was not printed until 1582 (Seville), and not in English until 1859. The popular Renaissance image had already been fixed by Mexía (1540), Perondinus (1553) and others.
3What is the evidence for Bayezid's iron cage, and how should the story be classified?
Answer. Bayezid's capture at Ankara and his death in captivity (March 1403) are certain. The cage is not confirmed by contemporary evidence. Timurid court histories describe courteous treatment. Some Ottoman chroniclers (for example Neşri) mention a kafes, whose meaning is debated. Latin writers such as Aeneas Silvius (Pius II) and later versions of Spandounes elaborated the humiliations. It should be treated as a legend that developed in the retelling (Milwright and Baboula 2011).
4Name Marlowe's main sources for Tamburlaine and one major change he made to the historical Timur.
Answer. Pedro Mexía's Silva de varia lección (1540), known to him through Fortescue's The Foreste (1571) and Whetstone's English Myrror (1586); Perondinus's Latin Vita (1553); and Ortelius's atlas (1570) for geography. Changes include making Timur a low-born pagan "Scythian shepherd" rather than a Muslim Barlas nobleman, and inventing most of the minor characters.
5What does the phrase "scourge of God" imply about Tamburlaine's role, and why is it double-edged?
Answer. It presents him as God's instrument for punishing the wicked (in the play, above all the Turks). But a scourge is only a tool that can be discarded, and in Part 2 Tamburlaine's defiance of God, including burning the Qur'an and claiming to be greater than God, is followed by his sickness and death. The phrase lets the play both glorify and limit him.
6How did Nicholas Rowe's Tamerlane (1701) use Timur for English politics?
Answer. Rowe, a Whig, made Tamerlane a moderate, tolerant, lawful monarch standing for William III, and Bajazet a tyrant standing for Louis XIV, as war with France approached. The play was staged every year around 4 November (William's birthday) and 5 November (his landing in 1688). It was not performed in London under the Tory ministry of 1710–14 and caused a riot in Dublin in 1712.
7Contrast Voltaire's and Gibbon's handling of the cage story.
Answer. Voltaire (Essai sur les mœurs, 1756, ch. 88) noted that no Persian or Arab life of Timur mentions the cage, only the Turkish annals, and suspected hostility or copying from Greek writers. He also called the related marriage story a fable. Gibbon (Decline and Fall, ch. 65, 1788) admitted that modern writers rejected the cage but defended it with a "chain of witnesses" (Boucicault's biographer, Poggio, Ibn Arabshah, Phrantzes, the Turkish annals). He was counting witnesses; Voltaire was weighing the kind of source.
8How does the post-1991 Uzbek image of Amir Temur differ from the European images, and what do they have in common?
Answer. The Uzbek image presents a state-builder, lawgiver and patron, the founding hero of the nation. It is marked by the Tashkent statue (1993) that replaced a Karl Marx monument, the "Year of Amir Temur" (1996) and the Timurid museum (1996). European images mostly made him a scourge, a moral lesson, an over-reacher, or a symbol of war. What they share is that each is a reinvention serving its makers' needs, whether Whig politics, humanist moralising, a critique of war, or national identity.

28 July 1402Battle of Ankara: Timur captures Bayezid; Castilian envoys present
Mar 1403Bayezid dies in captivity
15 June 1403John of Sultaniyya reaches Paris with Timur's letter to Charles VI
1403–06Clavijo's embassy, May 1403 to March 1406 (at Samarkand from 4 Sept to 21 Nov 1404)
Feb 1405Timur dies at Otrar
1427Schiltberger returns to Bavaria

c. 1447–48Poggio, De varietate fortunae
1450s–60sAeneas Silvius Piccolomini (Pius II), Asia

Data and map sources

  • Coastlines and lakes: Natural Earth (naturalearthdata.com, public domain), 1:50m land and 1:10m lakes, with the 1:10m historic Aral Sea shoreline. The Clavijo map also shows 1:10m rivers (today's courses). Both maps use an Albers equal-area conic projection. The map engine is the one built for The House of Timur, visual edition.
  • Historical borders: A. Ourednik, historical-basemaps (github.com/aourednik/historical-basemaps, GPL-3.0), 1400 layer ("Timurid Empire," "Castile," "France"), clipped to Natural Earth land. The project warns that its borders are approximate. The dataset's 1400 Ottoman and Byzantine outlines were left off because they look unreliable for that date. The text, not the outlines, carries the argument.
  • Routes: schematic lines through the places Clavijo names, in his order, with a few unlabelled bend points to keep sea legs at sea. They do not reconstruct the actual roads.
  • City positions: coordinates from English Wikipedia and Wikidata, rounded (for example Constantinople 41.01° N 28.98° E; Trebizond 41.01° N 39.73° E; Samarkand 39.65° N 66.97° E).
  • Chart: the timeline chart plots only the dates of works and events given in the text. No counts or other quantities are derived from it. A chart of "works per century" was considered and left out, because no published census of European works on Timur was found to base it on.
